flashcards.q: What is a VPC in the cloud?
flashcards.a: Your own closed, isolated network in the cloud. Inside it you create subnets and rules.
flashcards.more: It's like renting one floor of a building: the floor is yours, and other tenants can't walk in. Your servers, databases and load balancers all live inside the VPC.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a public and a private subnet?
flashcards.a: Servers in a public subnet can be reached directly from the internet. A private subnet has no direct route from outside.
flashcards.more: The usual layout is the load balancer in a public subnet and the app and database in private ones. A private server that needs to go out to the internet needs a NAT gateway.

flashcards.q: What does a security group do?
flashcards.a: It is the guard at a server's door: a list of which sources may reach which ports.
flashcards.more: Security groups are stateful, so the reply to an allowed incoming request leaves automatically. A rule can name another security group instead of an IP, which is both safer and simpler.

flashcards.q: What happens if you put 0.0.0.0/0 on a database's security group?
flashcards.a: The whole internet can knock on the database port. Bots find it within hours and start guessing passwords.
flashcards.more: The right way is to keep the database in a private subnet and allow only the app's security group. If you need to connect yourself, use a VPN or a bastion host.

flashcards.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
flashcards.a: Give each user or app only the permissions its job truly requires, and nothing more.
flashcards.more: Limit both the action and the resource: instead of "s3:*" and "*", name the specific actions and the specific bucket path. Then even a leaked key or a bug does limited damage.

flashcards.q: For an app, which is better: an IAM role or an access key?
flashcards.a: A role. Its temporary credentials rotate automatically and never have to sit in code or in a file.
flashcards.more: An access key is a permanent secret, and it's a disaster if it lands in git or a log. Attach a role to the app server or container and the SDK fetches temporary credentials by itself.

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between VMs, containers and serverless?
flashcards.a: Your responsibility shrinks in that order: a VM down to the OS, a container just the image and code, serverless just the function code.
flashcards.more: Less responsibility also means less control. Billing differs too: a VM is billed for the hours it is on, serverless only for the time it actually runs. For most Symfony APIs, containers are a good middle ground.

flashcards.q: In the shared responsibility model, what is the cloud's job and what is yours?
flashcards.a: The cloud: the building, hardware and hypervisor. You: data, IAM, network rules and backup testing.
flashcards.more: The more managed a service, the more layers the cloud handles (OS patches, DB patches). But responsibility for your data and access never becomes the cloud's.

flashcards.q: What is a cold start in serverless?
flashcards.a: The extra wait on the first call after a quiet spell, while the cloud boots your function from scratch.
flashcards.more: It can last from a fraction of a second to several seconds, depending on the runtime and the size of the code. You can pay to keep functions warm, but then you pay for idle time again. A container that is always on has no cold start.

flashcards.q: When is serverless more expensive than a container?
flashcards.a: When it is busy all the time. Per-run billing adds up, and a function that never rests can cost more than twice a container.
flashcards.more: As a rough picture at list prices: one vCPU of work for a whole month costs about 76 dollars on serverless and about 35 on an always-on container. The same function used lightly costs under a dollar. Check the current price page, because the shape matters more than the exact numbers.

flashcards.q: How do you keep serverless lock-in small?
flashcards.a: Keep the business logic in plain PHP classes, and make the cloud-specific handler a thin wrapper that only calls them.
flashcards.more: The trigger and handler format belong to one provider. If only a few lines of glue know about it, moving to containers means rewriting those lines, not the application.

flashcards.q: What backup settings must you choose yourself on a managed database?
flashcards.a: How many days of backups to keep, and a regular test restore. The cloud takes the backups, but these choices are yours.
flashcards.more: A retention of 1 day cannot undo a bad migration noticed after 3 days. Pick a retention longer than the time you might take to notice a mistake, and restore into a throwaway copy once a month to prove the backup works.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
flashcards.a: An image is a fixed package (code plus runtime) that never changes. A container is that image while it is running.
flashcards.more: You can run many containers from one image, like cooking many pots from one recipe. When a container dies, the files inside it are lost, but the image stays intact.

flashcards.q: What is a multi-stage build, and why use one?
flashcards.a: A Dockerfile with several stages, where only what you need from the earlier ones goes into the final image. That keeps the image small and safe.
flashcards.more: For Symfony, the first stage builds vendor with Composer, and the final stage holds only the PHP runtime and that vendor directory. Composer, git and dev dependencies never reach production.

flashcards.q: Why is deploying with the "latest" image tag a bad idea?
flashcards.a: Because "latest" keeps changing. You can't tell which code is running, and you can't go back to an earlier version.
flashcards.more: Tag every build with a version or git commit (shop-api:1.4.2). Then you know exactly which image runs in production, and a rollback just means going back to the earlier tag.

flashcards.q: Why run a container as a non-root user?
flashcards.a: If the app is hacked, the attacker still doesn't get root power, so the damage stays limited.
flashcards.more: Writing USER www-data in the Dockerfile makes the process run with limited rights. Give that user ownership only of the folders it must write to, such as var/.

flashcards.q: In Kubernetes, what do a Pod, a Deployment and a Service do?
flashcards.a: A Pod runs the container. A Deployment keeps a set number of Pods alive and rolls out new versions. A Service gives the Pods a stable address.
flashcards.more: Pods are short-lived: when one dies, its replacement gets a new IP. So nobody calls a Pod directly. Everyone calls the Service, which matches labels and forwards to healthy Pods.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a readiness and a liveness probe?
flashcards.a: Readiness asks whether the Pod is ready to take traffic. Liveness asks whether it is stuck, and if so it gets restarted.
flashcards.more: When readiness fails, the Pod is only taken out of the Service's list for a while. When liveness fails, the Pod is killed and replaced. A liveness probe shouldn't call an outside database.

flashcards.q: What is "click-ops", and what is wrong with it?
flashcards.a: Building infrastructure by clicking in the cloud console. Changes aren't recorded, it can't be rebuilt, and environments drift apart.
flashcards.more: The fix is Infrastructure as Code: the desired state of your infrastructure written as code, kept in git and reviewed. Then there is a history of who changed what, and if disaster strikes, one command brings everything back.

flashcards.q: Why are plan and apply separate in Terraform?
flashcards.a: Plan only shows what will change; apply actually changes it. Reviewing the plan first catches a mistaken delete or replace.
flashcards.more: The safest routine is to review the plan in a pull request, and after approval let CI apply that same plan. Keep the state file in an encrypted remote backend so the whole team sees the same state.

flashcards.q: How does Terraform show that someone changed infrastructure by hand in the console?
flashcards.a: terraform plan compares the real infrastructure with the code and lists every difference, so a hand-made change appears as a change to be undone.
flashcards.more: That is how drift is caught. The price: an emergency fix made in the console must be copied into the code, or the next apply will quietly undo it.

flashcards.q: When is Kubernetes more than you need?
flashcards.a: For one small app on one server. Docker Compose or a managed container service is simpler, because Kubernetes costs real time to learn and run.
flashcards.more: Kubernetes pays off with several services, several servers and a need for self-healing and gradual rollouts. Below that, its extra moving parts are cost without benefit.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between CI and CD?
flashcards.a: CI: build and test automatically on every push. CD: automatically (or with one click) ship code that passed to the servers.
flashcards.more: CI's central question is "did the code break anything?". CD's is "did the code reach users safely?". In continuous delivery the last step has a human approval; in continuous deployment even that is gone.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't you deploy by logging into the server and running git pull?
flashcards.a: Steps get forgotten, untested code can go live, servers end up different, and there is no way back.
flashcards.more: A pipeline runs the same steps in the same order every time and keeps a record of who deployed what. A hand deploy has neither.

flashcards.q: Why do cheap checks run first in a pipeline?
flashcards.a: Lint and static analysis take seconds. If they catch a mistake, you save the time of the slow tests and the build.
flashcards.more: The usual order: lint, static analysis, unit tests, integration tests, build, scan, deploy. The further right you go, the slower and costlier the check.

flashcards.q: What is a quality gate?
flashcards.a: A pipeline stage that blocks code from moving on to the next stage if it fails.
flashcards.more: For example, the build doesn't run if the tests fail, and the deploy doesn't run if the scan finds a serious vulnerability. A gate works only if a failure genuinely stops the pipeline.

flashcards.q: Why should CI tests run against a real MySQL?
flashcards.a: On a production-like database you catch the real behavior of SQL, indexes and migrations. SQLite behaves differently.
flashcards.more: GitHub Actions can start a MySQL container through services. Match the version to production as well (8.0 if production runs MySQL 8.0).

flashcards.q: What does "build once, promote the same artifact" mean?
flashcards.a: The image is built only once, and that same image moves from staging to production. Only the config changes, never the code.
flashcards.more: So what you tested and what you run are always identical. Build again for each environment and newer dependency versions can slip in and change the result.

flashcards.q: What does environment parity mean?
flashcards.a: Keeping staging and production as alike as possible: the same image, the same PHP and database versions. Only config, secrets and data differ.
flashcards.more: If the versions differ, passing in staging doesn't mean passing in production. Config differs through ENV variables, and is never written inside the image.

flashcards.q: What do you need in order to roll back quickly?
flashcards.a: The previous image intact in the registry, commit-hash tags, and backward-compatible migrations.
flashcards.more: In Kubernetes, `kubectl rollout undo` returns to the previous Deployment with one command. But if a migration dropped an old column, the app won't run even after the code goes back, so a migration should add first and delete later.

flashcards.q: How do you rename a database column without breaking rollback?
flashcards.a: Expand, then contract: add the new column and write to both, switch reads over, and drop the old column in a later release.
flashcards.more: A one-step rename leaves old code looking for a column that no longer exists, so rolling back swaps one outage for another. The price is three releases instead of one, which is why you use it only for changes that must be rollback-safe.

flashcards.q: What does FinOps mean?
flashcards.a: Engineers, finance and the business working together to understand, split and control cloud costs.
flashcards.more: The core idea: cost isn't only the finance department's worry. The engineer who creates a resource is the one making the cost decision, so cost has to be visible to them too.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable cloud costs?
flashcards.a: Fixed costs come whenever something is on (nodes, a database). Variable costs grow with use (data transfer, logs, storage).
flashcards.more: Double the orders and variable costs roughly double while fixed costs stay the same for now. But once you cross a limit and need another node or a bigger database, fixed costs rise in steps.

flashcards.q: How do you build a cost model?
flashcards.a: Split the cost into components (compute, database, network...), write down the basis for each, and separate fixed from variable.
flashcards.more: Compare the model with the real bill every month. A gap means there is a cost you don't know about. A model lets you answer "how much if orders double?" before the bill arrives.

flashcards.q: What is unit economics, and how is it measured in the cloud?
flashcards.a: The cost per unit of business, such as cloud cost per 1,000 orders = month's total cost ÷ orders × 1,000.
flashcards.more: If the total bill rises but the unit cost falls, the business is healthy. If orders grow only slightly but the unit cost jumps, waste has crept in somewhere and needs investigating.

flashcards.q: Why do cloud resources need tags?
flashcards.a: To split the bill between teams, services and environments. Without tags, "whose cost is this?" has no answer.
flashcards.more: Terraform's default_tags can put team, service and env on every resource. In billing you must also activate the tag as a cost allocation tag, or it won't show up in reports.

flashcards.q: Why is a FORECASTED budget alert better than an ACTUAL one?
flashcards.a: FORECASTED warns you early that, at this pace, you will pass the limit by month end. ACTUAL fires only after you hit it, when the money is gone.
flashcards.more: Teams usually set both: 80% forecast and 100% actual. It's best to send the alert to the team's chat channel so somebody sees it.

flashcards.q: Which workloads are safe to run on spot instances?
flashcards.a: Work that can be retried: queue workers, batch jobs, image processing. Not databases or web Pods.
flashcards.more: Spot is cheap, but the cloud can take it back at any time. If a worker's job is idempotent and sits in a queue, another worker simply picks it up when one dies.

flashcards.q: What must you not cut when reducing costs?
flashcards.a: Backups, multi-AZ, monitoring and alerts. These aren't waste, they are insurance.
flashcards.more: Waste is whatever nobody is using (idle disks, oversized instances, too many logs). Protection is what rescues you in a crisis. One incident can cost more than a whole year of savings.

flashcards.q: A private app pulls many GB from S3 and the NAT gateway line explodes. What is the cheap fix?
flashcards.a: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint. S3 traffic then skips the NAT gateway, so its per-GB charge disappears.
flashcards.more: The gateway endpoint for S3 is free. It works only for S3 and DynamoDB in the same region, so other internet traffic still uses the NAT gateway. In the story, the extra $780 was roughly 15 TB at about 5 cents per GB.

flashcards.q: How do you stop debug logs from inflating the bill in a Symfony app?
flashcards.a: Set the production Monolog handler to level info, and give the log group a short retention such as 7 days.
flashcards.more: The price is losing debug detail, so switch to debug only while investigating one incident. Keep audit and payment logs in a separate group with a longer retention.

flashcards.q: What is a hallucination?
flashcards.a: A model confidently making up wrong information it doesn't know, with no error at all.
flashcards.more: An LLM mainly predicts the "next likely word"; it doesn't check what is true. So for things like policy, prices and legal facts, take the answer from your own reliable data, not from the model's memory.

flashcards.q: What is LLM non-determinism, and does temperature 0 remove it?
flashcards.a: The same question gets a slightly different answer each time. Temperature 0 reduces it but doesn't guarantee an identical answer.
flashcards.more: That is why an LLM test doesn't match each answer exactly. It checks whether the overall accuracy across many examples stays above a threshold.

flashcards.q: Why treat an LLM call as a flaky outside service?
flashcards.a: It is slow (seconds), costly (per token), sometimes fails (rate limits, timeouts) and doesn't throw an exception when it is wrong.
flashcards.more: So it needs what any outside API needs: timeouts, a retry limit, a fallback, logs and cost monitoring. On top of that, it needs output validation.

flashcards.q: How is the cost of an LLM call calculated?
flashcards.a: Input and output tokens are counted separately: (input tokens × price) + (output tokens × price). Output usually costs more.
flashcards.more: For example, 500 input + 100 output tokens at $3 and $15 per million is $0.003 per call, or $300 for 100,000 calls a month. Smaller models, a max_tokens limit and caching cut the cost.

flashcards.q: Why must you validate an LLM's output before using it?
flashcards.a: A model can return broken JSON, unknown values or made-up facts. Without validation, they go straight into your system.
flashcards.more: In PHP, parse JSON with JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR, match the value with an enum's tryFrom, and put limits on numbers. If validation fails, take the fallback.

flashcards.q: What is the rule for personal data (PII) in prompts?
flashcards.a: Don't send what you can do without. Remove or replace phone numbers, emails, cards and Social Security numbers before sending.
flashcards.more: Whatever is in the prompt goes to the provider's servers. Sending only the fields you need is the safest approach; stripping with regexes doesn't catch every kind. Check the provider's data retention policy too.

flashcards.q: What is a golden set, and why does an LLM need one?
flashcards.a: A collection of hand-labeled real examples with correct answers, used to measure accuracy before and after a prompt or model change.
flashcards.more: It is the LLM's regression test. Include hard and ambiguous cases, and add mistakes caught in production. Change one thing at a time and measure again.

flashcards.q: What is prompt injection, and what is the strongest defense?
flashcards.a: Orders hidden in user text that the model takes as instructions. The strongest defense is minimal power for the model and human approval for money actions.
flashcards.more: Writing "don't obey instructions" in the prompt lowers the risk but doesn't stop it. So layer the guardrails: strip PII, separate instructions from data, minimal permissions, output validation, human approval.

flashcards.q: How do you stop a support bot from inventing answers about your policies?
flashcards.a: Ground it: put the real policy text in the prompt, tell it to answer only from that text, and give it a way to say "not in the policy".
flashcards.more: Hand the text to the model instead of trusting its memory, and route "not in the policy" to a person. Grounding lowers invention but does not remove it, so ask for the quoted sentence and keep the stored text up to date.
